name: Maximally Supersymmetric Plane Wave
description: A plane wave of ten dimensions, held up by the 5-form field of type IIB supergravity, that keeps all 32 of the theory's supersymmetries. It pulls every free particle toward its axis with one period in all eight directions across it. Matthias Blau, José Figueroa-O'Farrill, Christopher Hull, and George Papadopoulos found it in 2001, and it is the geometry near a light ray circling the sphere of anti-de Sitter space times a 5-sphere.
convention: We keep factors of $c$ explicit. The Ricci tensor is the standard contraction, $R_{\mu\nu} = R^\lambda{}_{\mu\lambda\nu}$.
history: Michel Cahen and Nolan Wallach came to this geometry through Huygens' principle, which holds in a spacetime where a flash of light travels on a sharp front with nothing trailing behind it [cahen1970]. In a short note of 1970 they sorted every Lorentzian symmetric space, a spacetime whose curvature is carried unchanged along every geodesic, and found that those which are not products of smaller ones come in two kinds [cahen1970]. One kind is de Sitter and anti-de Sitter space [cahen1970, blau2002]. The other is a single family of plane waves, each fixed by a symmetric matrix that says how hard the wave pulls toward its axis, or pushes away from it, in each direction across it, and in four dimensions these waves keep Huygens' principle [cahen1970, blau2002].¶Supergravity in ten or eleven dimensions has 32 supersymmetries, and a solution of it may keep all of them, some, or none [blau2002]. In eleven dimensions four kinds of solution keep all 32: flat space, anti-de Sitter space of four dimensions times a 7-sphere, anti-de Sitter space of seven dimensions times a 4-sphere, and a plane wave of Cahen and Wallach's family that Jerzy Kowalski-Glikman found in 1984 [blau2002, kowalski1984]. Type IIB supergravity in ten dimensions had only two, flat space and anti-de Sitter space of five dimensions times a 5-sphere [metsaev2002]. In October 2001 Matthias Blau, José Figueroa-O'Farrill, Christopher Hull, and George Papadopoulos put a plane wave of the same family into ten dimensions, held up by the theory's 5-form field, and found exactly one choice of its matrix that keeps all 32: a multiple of the identity, so that the wave pulls toward its axis equally in all eight directions across it [blau2002]. They called the physical significance of such waves "puzzling", since no brane was known to have one as a limit, the way anti-de Sitter space times a sphere is the throat of a stack of branes [blau2002, blau2002penrose].¶Where could such a wave come from? Back in 1976 Roger Penrose had shown that any spacetime has a plane wave as a limit: the neighbourhood of a single light ray, blown up without end, becomes a plane wave [penrose1976, blau2002penrose]. Eleven weeks after their first paper, Blau and his three coauthors took that limit of anti-de Sitter space times a sphere, along a light ray circling the sphere, and found the maximally supersymmetric waves, Kowalski-Glikman's from both solutions of eleven dimensions and their own from anti-de Sitter space of five dimensions times a 5-sphere [blau2002penrose]. Three weeks later David Berenstein, Juan Maldacena, and Horatiu Nastase posted the same limit as the geometry seen by "a particle that is moving very fast along the $S^5$", thanking Gary T. Horowitz for the idea and noting that the other paper had appeared while theirs was being written [berenstein2002]. Blau and his coauthors also showed how the limit squeezes the thirty symmetries of anti-de Sitter space times a 5-sphere into the wave's own thirty, a match they had called a coincidence in their first paper [blau2002, blau2002penrose].¶A free particle in the wave sits in a harmonic well, and light that leaves the axis comes back to it after a time $\pi/\mu c$, whatever direction it leaves in [berenstein2002, marolf2002]. A string sits in the same well, and in December 2001 Ruslan R. Metsaev wrote its action there and found it quadratic in every field in light cone gauge, so that "this model can be explicitly quantized", which the string in anti-de Sitter space times a sphere had resisted [metsaev2002]. Each of the eight directions across the wave becomes a massive field on the string, and so does each fermion [metsaev2002, berenstein2002]. Berenstein, Maldacena, and Nastase found the same spectrum in the gauge theory of four dimensions that Maldacena's correspondence pairs with anti-de Sitter space times a sphere, in long chains of one field with a few others set into them [berenstein2002, maldacena1998]. They summed a subset of its planar Feynman diagrams to get it, and called the result a "derivation" of the string spectrum from the gauge theory [berenstein2002].¶Where, then, is infinity in a spacetime that pulls everything back toward its axis? Berenstein and Nastase mapped the wave onto the Einstein static universe, a cylinder of time over a 9-sphere, and found that it covers the whole cylinder but one line [berenstein2002holography]. That line, the conformal boundary of the wave, is a single light ray winding round a great circle of the sphere for ever, and they took its one dimension as a sign that the holographic partner of the wave is a quantum mechanics, a matrix model with a single time [berenstein2002holography, marolf2002]. Donald Marolf and Simon F. Ross reached the same line from the causal structure alone, and found it to be the past boundary of the wave and its future boundary at once, so that a signal can go out to infinity and come back [marolf2002]. No plane wave is globally hyperbolic, a fact Penrose proved in 1965, and this one is no exception: no single moment of space holds the data for all of it [penrose1965plane, hubeny2002]. Veronika E. Hubeny and Mukund Rangamani argued that no pp-wave can have an event horizon, so that no Penrose limit of another spacetime can hold a black hole [hubeny2002].

related.text: Anti-de Sitter space of five dimensions times a 5-sphere, the throat of a stack of three-branes. Its Penrose limit along a light ray circling the sphere is this wave [blau2002penrose, berenstein2002].
Lin, Lunin, and Maldacena's droplets. A black half plane on their plane of droplets is this wave, and zooming in on the border of any droplet gives it back [lin2004].

Anti-de Sitter space of four dimensions times a 7-sphere, which keeps all the supersymmetry of eleven dimensions. The same limit along a light ray circling its sphere gives the plane wave of eleven dimensions that Kowalski-Glikman found, the counterpart of this one [blau2002penrose, kowalski1984].

The plane-fronted waves of four dimensions. This one is their homogeneous kin in ten, with $H = -\mu^2\left(x_1^2 + \dots + x_8^2\right)$ the same in every direction across it and a 5-form field to hold it up [blau2002].

Bonnor's beam of light, whose profile inside the beam is quadratic and the same in both directions across it, as this wave's is in all eight. Light sent against the beam swings through its axis as light swings through this wave's [bonnor1969light, marolf2002].

Anti-de Sitter space alone. A light ray of anti-de Sitter space times a sphere that does not move on the sphere has flat space for its Penrose limit, and only a ray circling the sphere gives this wave [blau2002penrose].

coordinates.name: Brinkmann

parameters.description: The mass of the wave, an inverse length. In the Brinkmann chart the five-form is $F = 2\mu c\,du\wedge\left(dx_1\wedge dx_2\wedge dx_3\wedge dx_4 + dx_5\wedge dx_6\wedge dx_7\wedge dx_8\right)$, normalised as Metsaev normalises it, so that its square carries the one component $R_{uu} = 8\mu^2$ of the Ricci tensor; the dilaton is constant and every other field vanishes

coordinates.convention: We use coordinates $(u, v, x_1, \dots, x_8)$, with $u$ the time that labels the wave fronts, carrying dimensions of time, $v$ a length along the rays, and $x_1$ to $x_8$ the eight lengths across them. We take components in the chart $x^0 = cu$, and a dot in the geodesic equations is a derivative with respect to an affine parameter, so $\dot{u}$ means $d(cu)/d\lambda$.

coordinates.name: Rosen

parameters.description: The mass of the wave, an inverse length. In the Brinkmann chart the five-form is $F = 2\mu c\,du\wedge\left(dx_1\wedge dx_2\wedge dx_3\wedge dx_4 + dx_5\wedge dx_6\wedge dx_7\wedge dx_8\right)$, normalised as Metsaev normalises it, so that its square carries the one component $R_{uu} = 8\mu^2$ of the Ricci tensor; the dilaton is constant and every other field vanishes

coordinates.convention: We use coordinates $(u, v, y_1, \dots, y_8)$, with $u$ a time and $v$ a length, and $y_1$ to $y_8$ lengths that label the light rays leaving the axis at $u = 0$, $x_i = y_i\sin(\mu cu)$ in the Brinkmann chart. We take components in the chart $x^0 = cu$, and a dot in the geodesic equations is a derivative with respect to an affine parameter, so $\dot{u}$ means $d(cu)/d\lambda$.
coordinates.line_element: ds^2 = -2c\,du\,dv + \sin^2\left(\mu cu\right)\left(dy_1^2 + dy_2^2 + dy_3^2 + dy_4^2 + dy_5^2 + dy_6^2 + dy_7^2 + dy_8^2\right)

coordinates.name: Conformally Flat

parameters.description: The mass of the wave, an inverse length. In the Brinkmann chart the five-form is $F = 2\mu c\,du\wedge\left(dx_1\wedge dx_2\wedge dx_3\wedge dx_4 + dx_5\wedge dx_6\wedge dx_7\wedge dx_8\right)$, normalised as Metsaev normalises it, so that its square carries the one component $R_{uu} = 8\mu^2$ of the Ricci tensor; the dilaton is constant and every other field vanishes

coordinates.convention: We use coordinates $(U, V, X_1, \dots, X_8)$, with $U$ a time, $\mu cU = \tan(\mu cu)$ for the $u$ of the Brinkmann chart, and $V$ and $X_1$ to $X_8$ lengths, $x_i = X_i\cos(\mu cu)$, so that the chart covers $|\mu cu| < \pi/2$. We take components in the chart $x^0 = cU$, and a dot in the geodesic equations is a derivative with respect to an affine parameter, so $\dot{U}$ means $d(cU)/d\lambda$.
